style: Comprehensive meaningful blend (interpretive text) + amplified study form; bare-transliteration in amp with Strong's carried in notes (matching the ch.1 pilot); em-dashes used sparingly.
chapterNote: Chapter 5 is the father's first sustained warning against the 'strange woman' and a corresponding call to delight in one's own wife. It moves in four movements: a summons to listen closely (vv. 1-2); the honeyed lips of the seductress whose end is bitter wormwood and whose feet sink down to death (vv. 3-6); the bitter accounting of the man who would not heed -- lost honor, lost years, public ruin, and a deathbed full of regret (vv. 7-14); the bright counter-call to drink water from one's own cistern and rejoice in the wife of one's youth (vv. 15-20); and a closing reminder that the LORD sees every path, and the wicked are bound and strangled by the very cords of their own sin (vv. 21-23).

1.text: My son, give heed to my wisdom; turn your ear to my understanding,
1.amp: My son [ben], give heed [qashab -- prick up the ear, listen with full attention] to my wisdom [chokmah]; turn [natah -- bend, stretch toward] your ear [ozen] to my understanding [tebunah],
1.notes: qashab (H7181) is the leaning-in, alert listening that refuses to miss a word; natah (H5186) is to bend the ear deliberately toward the speaker. As in chapter 2, wisdom asks the whole posture of the body -- ear bent, attention fixed -- before the warning even begins.

2.text: that you may guard sound discretion, and that your lips may keep knowledge.
2.amp: that you may guard [shamar -- keep, watch over, preserve] sound discretion [mezimmah -- the foreseeing, planning mind], and that your lips [saphah] may keep [natsar -- guard as a sentry] knowledge [daat].
2.notes: mezimmah (H4209) is the power to plan ahead -- a 'gray' word that elsewhere serves evil scheming, but ruled by wisdom it becomes the discretion that guards a man. shamar (H8104) and natsar (H5341) are paired sentry-verbs: discretion is to be guarded in the heart, and knowledge stationed on the very lips so that speech itself does not betray him.

3.text: For the lips of the forbidden woman drip honey, and her mouth is smoother than oil;
3.amp: For the lips [saphah] of the strange woman [zur -- the woman outside the bounds of covenant marriage] drip [nataph -- ooze, drop down] honey, and her mouth [chek -- literally the palate, the roof of the mouth] is smoother [chalaq -- slippery, flattering] than oil [shemen];
3.notes: zur (H2114) names her 'strange' not by race but by being off-limits -- another man's or no man's. chalaq (H2509) is to make smooth: her speech is frictionless and slippery, the opposite of wisdom's bracing but wholesome words. The honey on her lips is the bait; the next verse springs the trap.

4.text: but her aftermath is bitter as wormwood, sharp as a two-edged sword.
4.amp: but her end [acharit -- her latter outcome, what she comes to in the end] is bitter [mar] as wormwood [laanah -- the bitter desert herb, byword for poison and grief], sharp as a two-edged sword [literally a 'sword of mouths' -- a blade with two cutting edges].
4.notes: acharit (H319) is the 'latter end,' the final reckoning of a course of life -- a key word in this chapter (cf. v.11). laanah (H3939), wormwood, is Scripture's standard image for bitter consequence (Deut 29:18; Jer 9:15). The Hebrew 'sword of mouths' (a blade with two edges) plays grimly on her flattering mouth in v.3: the smooth mouth conceals a cutting one.

5.text: Her feet go down to death; her steps take hold of Sheol.
5.amp: Her feet [regel] go down [yarad -- descend, sink down] to death [mavet]; her steps lay hold [tamak -- grasp, take firm hold of, support themselves] on Sheol [sheol -- the grave, the realm of the dead].
5.notes: yarad (H3381), to go down, traces the downward slope of the whole encounter -- honey at the lips, but the feet already descending. tamak (H8551) usually means to grasp or hold up; here her steps cling to Sheol (H7585) itself as their destination. The same verb returns in v.22, where the wicked is held fast by his own sin -- the seductress's path and the sinner's bondage share one grip.

6.text: She gives no thought to the level path of life; her ways wander, and she does not know it.
6.amp: Lest she should ponder [palas -- weigh, make level, consider carefully] the path [orach] of life [chay], her ways stagger [nua -- shake, wander, totter] so that she cannot know [yada] them.
6.notes: the verse pictures a woman who never weighs where her road leads: nua (H5128) is the unsteady tottering of a drunkard or a reed in the wind -- her ways have no fixed line. She is not merely wicked but lost, wandering a path she herself cannot map, and dragging her victims into the same disorientation (cf. v.21, where the LORD, by contrast, sees every path plainly).

7.text: Now therefore, my sons, listen to me, and do not turn aside from the words of my mouth.
7.amp: Now therefore, O children [ben], hear [shama -- hear, listen, obey] me, and do not depart [sur -- turn aside, swerve away] from the words [emer] of my mouth [peh].
7.notes: shama (H8085) is hearing that issues in obedience, not mere sound reaching the ear. sur (H5493), to turn aside, is the danger word: the son must not swerve from the father's words, for the next verses show that swerving toward her door is the first fatal step (v.8).

8.text: Steer your path wide of her, and never let your feet approach the entrance of her dwelling,
8.amp: Remove [rachaq -- put far away, keep a wide distance] your way [derek] far from her, and do not come near [qarav -- draw close, approach] the door [petach -- the opening, the entrance] of her house [bayith],
8.notes: rachaq (H7368), repeated for force, commands not management of temptation but flight from it -- widen the distance, route the road elsewhere. qarav (H7126) is even to approach the doorway; wisdom does not test how close one may safely stand, but keeps a man from the threshold entirely (cf. 4:15; Gen 39:10).

9.text: lest you hand over your dignity to others and your years to one who is cruel;
9.amp: lest you give [natan] your honor [hod -- splendor, vigor, the dignity of a man in his prime] to others [acher], and your years [shanah] to the cruel one [akzari -- merciless, pitiless];
9.notes: hod (H1935) is the bloom and vigor of a man's strength, his good name and prime years -- all of it squandered and handed to strangers. akzari (H394) is the merciless creditor, husband, or disease that collects the debt; the pleasures cost everything a man has worth giving, and the collector shows no pity.

10.text: lest strangers be filled with your strength, and your hard-won labors end up in an alien's house.
10.amp: lest strangers [zur] be filled [saba -- be glutted, satisfied to the full] with your wealth [koach -- literally your strength, your earning power], and your toils [etseb -- painful labor, what you sweat for] enrich the house [bayith] of a foreigner [nokri];
10.notes: koach (H3581) is raw strength used here for the wealth that strength produces -- the years of a man's vigor consumed by outsiders who give nothing back. etseb (H6089) is labor wrung out in pain; the tragedy is that all this hard-bought substance ends up provisioning a stranger's household rather than his own (the opposite of the blessed home in vv.15-19).

11.text: and at the last you groan, when your flesh and your body are consumed,
11.amp: and you mourn [naham -- groan, growl in pain like a wounded beast] at your latter end [acharit], when your flesh [basar] and your body are consumed [kalah -- spent, finished, brought to an end],
11.notes: naham (H5098) is the low groan of an animal in pain -- the deathbed sound of a man whose vigor is gone. acharit (H319), 'latter end,' echoes v.4: her end was bitter wormwood, and now his end is a wasted body. kalah (H3615) means utterly spent -- the strength given to strangers in v.10 is the strength now consumed out of his own frame.

12.text: and you say, "How I hated discipline, and my heart spurned correction!
12.amp: and you say [amar], "How I have hated [sane -- detested, been hostile to] instruction [musar -- corrective discipline], and my heart [leb] despised [naats -- spurned, treated with contempt] reproof [tokachat -- rebuke, correction];
12.notes: the deathbed confession names the root: not weakness but hatred. musar (H4148) is the formative correction the prologue prized (1:2-3, 8); naats (H5006) is the strongest verb for contemptuous rejection. The same scorn the fool of chapter 1 had for wisdom now returns as the dying man's self-indictment.

13.text: I would not heed the voice of my teachers, nor turn my ear to those who instructed me.
13.amp: neither have I obeyed [shama] the voice [qol] of my teachers [yarah -- those who taught, literally those who 'pointed the way'], nor bent [natah] my ear [ozen] to my instructors [lamad -- those who trained me];
13.notes: yarah (H3384), to teach, is the root behind torah, instruction -- and it pictures pointing or shooting an arrow toward a mark. natah (H5186) deliberately reverses v.1: the son was told to bend his ear toward wisdom, and the ruined man confesses he refused to bend it at all. The remedy was offered; the refusal was his own.

14.text: I am at the very brink of utter ruin, in the midst of the assembled congregation."
14.amp: I was nearly [meat -- within a little, on the very edge] in all evil [ra] in the midst [tavek] of the congregation [qahal] and assembly [edah].
14.notes: meat (H4592) means 'within a hair's breadth' -- he stands at the brink of total disgrace. The sting is the setting: 'in the midst of the qahal (H6951) and edah (H5712),' the gathered covenant community -- his private sin has become public scandal, his shame exposed before the very assembly where God's people gather (cf. the public exposure of v.9).

15.text: Drink water from your own cistern, fresh running water from your own well.
15.amp: Drink [shatah] waters from your own cistern [bor -- the hewn pit that holds gathered water], and running waters [nazal -- flowing, trickling streams] from your own well [beer -- the dug well, the living spring].
15.notes: the chapter pivots from warning to invitation, and the image is water -- life, refreshment, and in the dry land, covenant blessing. bor (H953) is the household cistern and beer (H875) the dug well; nazal (H5140) is fresh flowing water, not the stagnant kind. Marital love is pictured as one's own pure spring, satisfying and lawfully owned -- the answer to the borrowed honey of v.3.

16.text: Should your springs spill out into the streets, your channels of water in the public squares?
16.amp: Let your fountains [maayan -- springs, sources] be dispersed [puts -- scattered, spilled] abroad [chuts -- outside, into the open street], and rivers of waters in the streets [rechob -- the broad public squares]?
16.notes: read as a pointed question (as the flow demands): why let the wellspring meant for one's own home gush out into public streets, squandered on every passerby? The spilling spring is the picture of a man's vitality and offspring dissipated in promiscuity (cf. the strangers who drain his strength in v.10); the next verse gives the answer -- keep them your own.

17.text: Let them be yours alone, and not shared with strangers beside you.
17.amp: Let them be for yourself alone, and not for strangers [zur] with you.
17.notes: the answer to v.16: the spring is to belong to one household, not to outsiders. zur (H2114) is the same 'strange' root that named the seductress in v.3 -- the contrast is exact. What is faithfully kept within the marriage is fruitful; what is scattered to strangers is lost. Faithfulness is not deprivation but possession.

18.text: May your wellspring rest under God's blessing, and take your gladness in the bride of your early years --
18.amp: Let your fountain [maqor -- spring, source, wellspring] be blessed [barak], and rejoice [samach -- be glad, take delight] in the wife [ishshah] of your youth [neurim -- the years of early manhood].
18.notes: maqor (H4726) is the source-spring, here a tender figure for marriage and its fruitfulness, and it is to be barak (H1288), set under God's blessing. 'The wife of your youth' (neurim, H5271) is the bride of one's early years, to be loved across a lifetime; samach (H8055) commands gladness -- marital love is not merely permitted but enjoined as joy (cf. Eccl 9:9; Mal 2:14-15).

19.text: a loving doe, a graceful mountain deer; let her breasts fill you with delight at all times, and be captivated always in her love.
19.amp: a loving [ahavah] doe [ayyelet -- a female deer] and a graceful [chen -- favor, beauty, charm] roe [yaalah -- a mountain ewe-deer]; let her breasts satisfy [ravah -- drench, saturate, give to drink one's fill] you at all times [et], and be ravished [shagah -- be intoxicated, swept away, lost in] always [tamid -- continually] in her love [ahavah].
19.notes: the doe and the mountain deer are images of grace, gentleness, and beauty; ravah (H7301), to drench or water, ties the verse back to the spring imagery of v.15 -- she is the well that satisfies. shagah (H7686) means to be intoxicated or to go astray; here the only sanctioned 'going astray' is a man losing himself in his own wife's love -- the very same verb is turned against the adulterer in v.20 and the fool in v.23. tamid (H8548) is the word for the continual offering: this delight is to be perpetual.

20.text: Why then, my son, be intoxicated with a forbidden woman, and embrace the bosom of a stranger?
20.amp: And why will you, my son [ben], be ravished [shagah -- intoxicated, swept away -- the same verb as v.19] with a strange woman [zur], and embrace [chabaq -- clasp, fold in your arms] the bosom [cheq -- the lap, the embrace] of a foreigner [nokri]?
20.notes: shagah (H7686) deliberately echoes v.19: the same intoxication that belongs rightly to the wife of one's youth is here squandered on the strange woman (zur, H2114). The father's argument is not 'no pleasure' but 'why this pleasure, when the better and lawful one is yours?' Sin is here exposed as foolish exchange -- trading the satisfying spring for a stranger's poisoned cup.

21.text: For a man's ways are before the eyes of the LORD, and He weighs out all his paths.
21.amp: For the ways [derek] of a man [ish] are before [nokach -- right in front of, full in view] the eyes [ayin] of the LORD [YHWH], and He ponders [palas -- weighs, makes level, examines] all his tracks [magal].
21.notes: the decisive motive: every secret path lies open before the LORD (H3068). palas (H6424), to weigh or make level, is the very verb the wandering woman would not apply to her own way in v.6 -- she never weighed her path, but God weighs every man's. Nothing done in the dark of her house (v.8) escapes His level gaze; private sin is conducted in the full sight of God.

22.text: His own iniquities trap the wicked man; he is held fast by the cords of his sin.
22.amp: His own iniquities [avon -- guilt, perversity and its punishment] shall ensnare [lakad -- catch as in a net or trap] the wicked [rasha] himself, and he shall be held fast [tamak -- gripped, taken firm hold of] with the cords [chebel -- ropes, binding tethers] of his sin [chattath].
22.notes: sin needs no external executioner: avon (H5771) hunts down the very man who committed it. lakad (H3920) is to be caught in one's own trap, and tamak (H8551) echoes v.5 -- the seductress's steps laid hold of Sheol, and now her victim is held fast by the cords of his own sin. chebel (H2256) are binding ropes; the man who chased freedom in forbidden pleasure is bound hand and foot by it.

23.text: He will die for want of discipline, and in the greatness of his folly he goes astray.
23.amp: He shall die [muth] for lack of instruction [musar -- corrective discipline]; and in the greatness [rob -- abundance, multitude] of his folly [ivvelet] he shall go astray [shagah -- stagger off, be lost -- the same verb as vv.19-20].
23.notes: the chapter ends where the deathbed of v.12 pointed: the man dies for want of the musar (H4148) he hated. ivvelet (H200) is moral folly, the willful stupidity that despises correction. shagah (H7686) closes the chapter's wordplay with bitter irony -- the intoxication meant for the marriage bed (v.19) becomes, untethered, the staggering of a man lost beyond recovery. Folly does not merely err; it loses its way and dies.
